issues.issue: The Effective Date is left blank ("as of the _ day of [ ]"), so the date from which the Agreement and its representations run cannot be fixed from the text. That blank is a mechanical defect a court would have to fill by construction.
The undefined Effective Date matters because Section 3's chapeau makes the Company's representations effective "as of the Effective Date"; but this is a gap rather than a contradiction.

Undefined terms are given the Operating Agreement's meanings, while paragraph 5.1 supplies its own definitions of "Affiliate" and related terms "for purposes of this Article 5 and elsewhere as specified", leaving which definition governs elsewhere unresolved. A court could be asked to reconcile the preamble with 5.1.

"Notes shall be purchased in units of $1.00" and a minimum of "20,000 Units or U.S. $20,000" use "Units", a term not defined in this Agreement. The reference is thin but the arithmetic makes its meaning plain.

"Loan Amount" is defined as the amount required to be loaned, yet the same paragraph makes it adjustable for "the accrual and payment of interest and principal", so it is unclear whether Loan Amount tracks principal or a running balance. Because payments under 1.4(c) turn on "relative principal amounts", the distinction has consequences.

The roll-over right is conditioned on the Noteholder being a "qualified investor at the time of the request", a term used but never defined in the Agreement (Section 4.1 uses "accredited investor" instead). A court would have to decide which standard governs.

The "Floating Rate" is set unilaterally "in the sole discretion of the Company" subject to quarterly adjustment, but the floor is stated as "not less than eight percent (8.00%) on an annualized basis for such calendar year", mixing a quarterly reset with an annual measuring period. Whether the 8% floor is tested quarterly or over the calendar year is genuinely uncertain.

Prepayment on request is available "on the last day of any quarter during or after which all of the following conditions have been satisfied", which is awkward as to whether conditions must be met before or within the quarter. The ambiguity is small but real.

The condition turns on the Company's "sole and absolute discretion" that prepayment "will not adversely affect the Company's obligations or liquidity", a standard with no benchmark and no good-faith qualifier. A court could be asked whether any implied limit constrains that discretion.

The paragraph refers to "the Holding Period", whereas 1.4(a)(ii)(A) defines only a "Minimum Holding Period"; the mismatched term is a mechanical slip. Its meaning is nonetheless recoverable from context.

Selective prepayment of certain Noteholders' Notes sits against the ratable-payment covenant in 6.1(b) and the pro rata rule in 1.4(c), though both are expressed as subject to 1.4. The carve-out largely resolves the tension.

The pro rata payment rule is made "subject to" 1.4(a)-(b), which permit wholly discretionary and selective prepayments, so the rule can be displaced at will. A court could be asked how far 1.4(b) may swallow 1.4(c) and 6.1(b).

The proviso protects a Noteholder against an amendment with "discriminatory application" to his Note, a phrase that is nowhere defined and could cover any non-uniform effect. The scope of that protection is genuinely contestable.

This 50%-of-principal amendment mechanic for the Notes sits alongside paragraph 10.5, which requires Company approval and a "Majority in Interest" for modifications of the Agreement, and the two consent regimes could overlap. The subject matters differ, which mostly reconciles them.

The clause says the Company may re-issue Notes "and then only upon the condition that the original Note is returned", which sits oddly with the following sentence requiring issuance of a replacement for a lost or destroyed Note. The reader must decide whether the return condition applies to replacements too.

The Closing Account must be "segregated from the Company's general bank accounts" and held "exclusively" for investor funds, yet the same paragraph contemplates funds "held ... by the Company" during the Pre-Qualification Period. Whether segregation is absolute is arguable.

This paragraph speaks of amending the "proposed Note Subscription Amount" and returning funds exceeding the "Note Subscription Amount approved by the Company", while 2.2(a) frames subscription and acceptance in terms of the "Loan Amount". The two labels are used interchangeably without a stated equivalence.

The Schedule is called "SCHEDULE A" here but the preamble and paragraph 1.1 call it the "Schedule of Purchasers attached hereto", and the exhibit list names only a "Schedule of Purchasers". The inconsistent label is minor and readily harmonised.

The promise of a security interest in the Company's assets is qualified out of existence by 5.3(a), which lets the Manager grant liens senior to the Lien and subordinate Noteholder remedies. A court could be asked whether 2.3(a) leaves the Noteholders any secured position.

The clause subordinates "the lien on the Fund's assets", but "Fund" is not a defined term anywhere in the Agreement, which uses "Company" throughout. The slip is small but goes to the description of the collateral.

Blanket subordination to "any Company Borrowings" is hard to square with 6.2(b), which forbids the Company to permit any Lien on the Collateral without a Majority in Interest except as permitted with respect to a Company Borrowing. Which provision controls the extent of permitted senior liens is arguable.

This funding mechanic covers only commitments under 1.2(c) and 1.2(d), but 1.2(b) directs that Noteholder-requested increases be "funded as provided in paragraph 2.4 below". The cross-references do not match up.
The Company is a Delaware LLC yet the representation is of "requisite corporate power", a mismatch of legal vocabulary. It is a drafting slip unlikely to change meaning.

The representation covers "the Series of Notes to be issued in such closing", but "Series" is not a defined concept and the Agreement elsewhere treats the Notes as a single undifferentiated class. Whether Notes are issued in distinct series matters to ratable payment and voting.
The carve-out for violations "that would not have a material adverse effect on the Company" supplies no measure of materiality. Such qualifiers are standard but their boundary is contestable.

The purpose clause reaches "such other related activities" as the Manager "deems reasonably necessary or appropriate", a catch-all sitting against an enumerated list of lending and foreclosure activities. Its outer limit is uncertain.

The representation that Portfolio Loans are secured by property located "primarily in the United States" sits against 6.1(g), which contemplates loans where foreign-secured Portfolio Loans exceed twenty percent. The two provisions pull in different directions on geography.

The covenant to use proceeds "solely for the operations of its business" is far narrower than 5.2, by which the Purchasers consent to use of proceeds "for any purpose not prohibited by the Operating Agreement". The two use-of-proceeds provisions are hard to reconcile.

The disclaimer that the Company and Manager "owe no fiduciary or similar duties" leaves the reach of "similar duties" undefined, and does not say whether it displaces implied covenants or duties arising under the Operating Agreement. That scope is exactly the sort of term litigants fight over.

A blanket no-duty statement is in tension with the express arm's-length and fairness obligations imposed on the Manager in 5.7(e), 5.8 and the covenants in 6.1. A court could be asked whether 4.3 nullifies those protections.

"Affiliate" turns on undefined "control", and the definition is expressly limited to "this Article 5 and elsewhere as specified in this Agreement" while "Affiliate" is used in 9(c) and 10.8 without any such specification. Both the control test and the definition's reach are open.

Excluding "any Noteholder or a limited partner or non-voting member of a Sponsored Investment Fund" from "Affiliate" cuts against 5.8's final sentence, which contemplates Noteholders who "are also Affiliates of the Manager or Servicer". The carve-out and that sentence do not sit easily together.

"Private Client" reaches "any investor or client or their Affiliates for whom the Manager or its Affiliates provides loan or real estate brokerage, investment or lending services", a boundary the Manager can enlarge simply by providing services. Because Private Client status switches off the restrictions in 5.7(b)(i)-(iii), the definition's reach matters.

"Sponsored Investment Fund" sweeps in any fund "sponsored, promoted, owned or managed now or in the future by the Manager or its Affiliates" and names R.E. Loans, LLC expressly, so the label attaches to the Manager's own affiliated vehicles. Whether that status was meant to strip such entities of affiliate treatment is genuinely contestable.

Because 5.7(e) excludes loans to a Sponsored Investment Fund from "Related Party Loan", this definition lets loans to the Manager's own affiliated funds escape the 20% cap in 5.7(e)(ii) and the arm's-length conditions in 5.7(e)(i). That is difficult to reconcile with the Agreement's evident scheme of restricting affiliate lending.

Consent is given to use of proceeds "for any purpose not prohibited by the Operating Agreement", an open-ended standard defined by reference to a separate document the Company may amend. The limit on the Company's use of investor money is therefore hard to locate.
This open consent is inconsistent with 3.8, under which the Company "shall use the proceeds of the Loan solely for the operations of its business". A court would have to decide which governs.

The clause says the Purchasers agree to "the provisions of paragraphs 5.2(a)-(f)", but paragraph 5.2 has no subparagraphs; the lettered provisions are in 5.3. That mis-citation leaves the object of the agreement to be supplied by construction.

The reference to authority "pursuant to the terms of the Operating Agreement and the Act" conflicts with paragraph 3.6, which defines "the Act" as the Securities Act of 1933, whereas here it must mean the Delaware LLC Act. The defined term and its use point in different directions.

The Manager may agree to whatever subordination and standstill terms it "may deem commercially reasonable", a self-judged standard with no external benchmark. Its content would be the battleground in any dispute about a subordination.

Authorising liens senior to the Lien and terms that "subordinate or otherwise restrict the rights of the Noteholders" is hard to reconcile with 2.3(a)'s grant of a security interest to the Noteholders and 6.2(b)'s prohibition on permitting Liens on the Collateral. Read at full width this paragraph can hollow out the security bargained for.

Transactions are permitted if "within the general scope and purpose of the Company", a boundary that is nowhere fixed and that the Manager judges in its sole discretion. The catch-all "or other persons" at the end of an enumerated list adds to the uncertainty.

The broad sole-discretion permission is qualified only by "except to the extent prohibited by this Agreement", leaving its relation to the specific affiliate conditions in 5.7 to be worked out. The specific conditions would normally prevail, which reduces the tension.

The unrestricted Co-Lending permission must be read with 6.1(f), which requires commercially reasonable efforts to prevent a Co-Lending Activity from constituting a security, and with 5.8's arm's-length proviso. The qualifier "except to the extent prohibited by this Agreement" mostly reconciles them.

This paragraph lets the Company sell foreclosed property to the Manager and Affiliates "on such terms and conditions as the Manager, in its sole discretion, determines", while 5.7(b) imposes marketing, pricing and commission conditions on precisely those sales. The general permission and the specific conditions must be reconciled.

Sole-discretion purchases and sales of Portfolio Loans with Affiliates sit against the specific pricing and underwriting conditions in 5.7(c) and 5.7(d) for the same transactions. The saving words "except to the extent prohibited by this Agreement" leave the relationship to be construed.

The cap on Loan Services compensation is measured by fees "payable pursuant to paragraphs 5.4(b)-(f)", yet 5.4 states those fees are payable to the Manager or its designee, not necessarily to the Servicer, and 5.6 lets Affiliates keep further compensation outright. Whether the cap is effective is arguable.

The chapeau says the Company "shall be entitled to pay" fees, which reads as a permission rather than an obligation, while the listed items are stated as fixed entitlements. Whether the fees are mandatory or discretionary is left open.

The fee list defines a "Management Fee" in 5.4(a), but 6.2(c) forbids paying salaries in any month in which a "Portfolio Management Fee" is payable, a term defined nowhere. The mismatch of labels affects when 6.2(c) bites.
